title: PortLog harness as the provider-neutral process platform
description:
## Destination

Produce an implementation-ready specification for narrowing apps/server around the PortLog harness: every agent-initiated operation runs through one provider/model-agnostic harness; projects, threads, SQLite, WebSocket delivery, settings, and durable history remain server infrastructure; model choice is a global app default applied per turn; provider credentials remain harness configuration.

## Notes

Planning-only wayfinder effort. Consult domain-modeling and grilling for unresolved product vocabulary. Research agent harnesses, Palantir Ontology/AIP, Pi/OMP, and durable execution patterns when needed. Do not make the model emit a universal operation-kind taxonomy unless a later decision proves it necessary. Human approval is not mandatory by default; autonomous authority is bounded by scoped capabilities, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, recovery, and audit.

## Decisions so far

- [Define the provider-neutral turn and harness session boundary](pl-217.1) — Threads are provider-agnostic durable identities; each user turn is a durable harness task run by an on-demand PortLog invocation, with persisted events and execution state used for recovery. Completion is policy-evaluated; no universal HarnessOperationKind.
- [Define the canonical harness event and operation trace](pl-217.2) — Use typed model/tool/logic_program invocations with durable semantic boundaries, replay and retry rules, rebuildable projections, and optional raw diagnostics rather than raw payloads by default.
- [Specify provider and settings migration to per-turn harness routing](pl-217.4) — Clean-slate target: global resolved model selection routes every turn through PortLog; invocation metadata preserves the execution snapshot, while threads remain provider-neutral.
- [Research autonomous PortLog authority without mandatory human approvals](pl-217.6) — Approval-free execution is bounded by scoped capabilities/identity, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, durable recovery, and audit; escalation remains optional.
- [Define harness authority, approvals, and infrastructure ownership](pl-217.5) — PortLog owns the complete agent loop and capability authority; server remains infrastructure and adapter layer; generic tools use declared capability scope and policy metadata instead of a premature domain ontology.
- [Define governed PortLog process actions versus discovered tools](pl-217.3) — Start with generic registry-backed tools; defer governed domain actions until a concrete capability needs stronger semantics.
- [Define WebSocket and UI projection for harness traces](pl-217.7) — Follow OMP: conversation-first UI with inline expandable activity; durable typed events drive projections, transient deltas stream live, and reconnect rebuilds from SQLite/event log.

## Not yet specified

<!-- no remaining specified frontier; future domain-action work graduates only when a concrete capability requires it -->

## Out of scope

- Rebuilding the Paper chat design.
- Deleting the apps/server infrastructure spine.
- Treating Claude, Codex, OpenCode, or any other provider session as a product concept.

title: Define the provider-neutral turn and harness session boundary
description: ## Question\nWhat is the canonical distinction between a durable chat/thread, a harness session, a turn, and a per-turn model execution when no thread is owned by a provider? Specify identity, lifecycle, restart/resume behavior, and what old provider fields mean.
close_reason: Decision resolved: provider-neutral durable turn and on-demand harness execution boundary

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): A thread/chat is the durable product identity and is provider-agnostic. Each user turn creates a durable harness task executed by an on-demand PortLog harness invocation; the invocation may be short-lived, crash, or be replaced. Persisted events and execution state are the recovery source. The model may declare completion, but the harness accepts completion only through the turn's completion policy: deterministic validators, human approval, or explicit terminal response can complete it; policy limits, cancellation, or unrecoverable errors can terminate it as cancelled or failed. No universal HarnessOperationKind is part of the canonical model; the trace records concrete model/tool calls, results, approvals, failures, retries, and model snapshots.

title: Define the canonical harness event and operation trace
description: ## Question\nWhat should SQLite and WebSocket persist and emit for a turn and its agent/tool activity? Compare Pi/OMP and managed-agent event-log patterns; decide whether a generic operation taxonomy is necessary or whether typed tool-call events plus lifecycle metadata are sufficient.
notes: Approved: shared invocation envelope with typed model/tool/logic_program targets; completed deterministic logic-program results replay; durable persistence uses stable invocation IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replay of completed invocations, policy-driven retry/resume, and rebuildable projections.
close_reason: Decision resolved: canonical durable harness trace and payload retention

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Use one invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets for model inference, external tools, and logic programs. They share correlation, lifecycle, timing, retry, and error mechanics but retain distinct execution semantics. No universal HarnessOperationKind. Completed logic-program invocations replay from their recorded result during recovery; interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic invocations may rerun under retry policy.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Durable event persistence uses stable invocation IDs and attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replay of completed invocations, policy-driven retry/resume for interrupted invocations, and projections that can be rebuilt from the event log.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): The canonical trace uses a shared invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets (model, tool, logic_program), stable invocation IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent append-only writes, replayable completed invocations, policy-driven retries for interrupted work, and rebuildable projections. Persist semantic event boundaries, checkpoints, lifecycle state, normalized results, and artifact references. Stream transient deltas to the UI but do not persist every token. Do not persist full raw model/tool payloads by default; support optional diagnostic/evaluation capture with retention and redaction controls.

title: Define governed PortLog process actions versus discovered tools
description: ## Question\nFor the initial PortLog architecture, should all capabilities remain generic registry-backed tools, with a future governed-action mechanism introduced only when a concrete process capability needs stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics? Avoid designing a full process ontology now.
close_reason: Decision resolved: generic capability registry and future governed actions

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Initial PortLog uses only generic registry-backed tools. Each tool declares capability scope and policy metadata. A governed domain-action mechanism may be introduced later only when a concrete process capability proves it needs stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics. Do not design a full process ontology now.

title: Specify provider and settings migration to per-turn harness routing
description: ## Question\nHow do existing ProviderKind, provider settings, credentials, model selections, and historical SQLite rows migrate to a global app-default model applied per turn while every agent action runs through PortLog? Define compatibility, fallback, and UI exposure.
notes: Clean-slate target; no legacy compatibility. Global app model default routes every turn through PortLog. Invocation retains standard durable-execution model snapshot and retry/usage metadata.
close_reason: Decision resolved: clean-slate per-turn harness routing and model metadata

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): Plan the clean-slate target architecture rather than an enduring legacy compatibility layer. Threads and sessions are provider-neutral; all new turns use the global app model default through PortLog; old provider-owned development data need not remain usable. Credentials remain harness configuration. Each model invocation retains standard durable-execution metadata: resolved model/provider route, relevant settings and configuration version, timing/usage metadata, and retry identity. This is execution metadata only, not thread identity or future routing state.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): The global app default stores a resolved model selection: provider route, model ID, and relevant model settings. Each turn snapshots that selection into model-invocation metadata; threads remain provider-neutral.

title: Define harness authority, approvals, and infrastructure ownership
description: ## Question\nWhich agent-initiated capabilities must be dispatched by PortLog, how are approvals/cancellation/retry/recovery governed, and which responsibilities remain direct server infrastructure (SQLite, WebSocket, settings, projects, user actions)?
notes: PortLog owns complete agent loop; no mandatory human approval gates. Approval-free execution is bounded by scoped capabilities/identity, deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, durable recovery, and audit. Need decide PortLog capability/action model.
close_reason: Decision resolved: PortLog authority and capability model

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): PortLog owns the complete per-turn agent loop: model invocation, context assembly, tool selection and dispatch, approvals, checkpoints, retries, cancellation, recovery, and completion. apps/server remains infrastructure and capability adapters; agent-originated effects cross the PortLog authority seam before server execution.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Decision (approved by user): No mandatory human approval gates. The nuanced authorization, safety, sandboxing, staging, reversibility, audit, and failure-policy design is intentionally delegated to a dedicated research ticket rather than collapsed into 'unconstrained execution'.

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): PortLog uses a capability registry plus generic tools. Each tool declares its capability scope and policy metadata; PortLog remains the complete-loop authority and applies deterministic policy, isolation, idempotency, reconciliation, recovery, and audit controls. Do not build a full domain-action registry or process ontology yet.

title: Research autonomous PortLog authority without mandatory human approvals
description: ## Question\nHow should PortLog safely and durably govern fully autonomous agent-originated work when human approval is never required by default? Research the user's existing work and relevant patterns for authorization, capability boundaries, sandboxing, policy evaluation, staging/reversibility, auditability, idempotency, failure containment, cancellation, and recovery. Distinguish harness authority from server infrastructure execution. Do not introduce a universal HarnessOperationKind taxonomy.
close_reason: Decision resolved: safety controls for approval-free autonomous execution

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Approval-free autonomous execution is acceptable when bounded by least-privilege capability manifests and scoped identities, deterministic policy gates outside the model, isolation for filesystem/network/process/secrets, idempotency keys for external side effects, explicit unknown outcomes with reconciliation before retry, checkpoints with bounded classified retries and compensation, and append-only audit evidence. Human escalation remains optional rather than a hidden prerequisite. Approval-free does not mean unrestricted execution.

title: Define WebSocket and UI projection for harness traces
description: ## Question\nHow should the provider-neutral durable harness trace be projected to the WebSocket/UI? Define live transient streaming versus durable semantic events, rebuild/reconnect behavior, turn state and invocation rendering, failure/unknown/retry visibility, and how existing orchestration projections are replaced or adapted. SQLite/event log remains authoritative; do not reintroduce provider identity or a universal HarnessOperationKind.
close_reason: Decision resolved: OMP-style WebSocket and UI projection

comments.author: vikramoddiraju
comments.text: Resolution (approved by user): Follow OMP-style projection. Conversation remains primary; model/tool/logic-program activity appears inline as expandable details/cards. The canonical typed durable events drive the UI, transient deltas stream live, SQLite/event log remains authoritative, and reconnect rebuilds durable state before resuming live delivery. No separate execution dashboard or universal HarnessOperationKind initially.

title: Implement PortLog as the provider-neutral durable harness
description:
## Problem Statement

PortLog currently sits behind a compatibility bridge in a server architecture whose product model is still organized around provider-specific sessions. That makes the application treat Claude, Codex, OpenCode, and other runtimes as the primary unit of work, even though PortLog's intended product is provider-neutral process engineering. The server must remain responsible for projects, provider-neutral chats/threads, SQLite persistence, settings, WebSocket delivery, and durable history, while every agent-initiated operation is executed through one PortLog harness.

## Solution

Make PortLog the single, provider- and model-agnostic agent harness. A thread is a durable chat identity, not a provider session. Each user message creates a durable turn task and invokes PortLog on demand. PortLog owns the complete agent loop: context assembly, per-turn model resolution, model inference, semantic tool selection, generic tool execution through registered capabilities, logic-program execution, retries, checkpoints, recovery, cancellation, and completion evaluation. Short-lived harness runtimes may be replaced or restarted; persisted turn state and the canonical event log are the recovery source.

The application stores a global resolved model selection—provider route, model ID, and relevant settings—and snapshots it into each model invocation for reproducibility. Existing provider-specific development data is not a compatibility requirement. Credentials remain harness configuration. The UI follows an OMP-style conversation-first presentation with inline expandable activity details.

## User Stories

1. As a process engineer, I want to start a chat without choosing a provider-owned session type, so that the chat represents my work rather than a vendor runtime.
2. As a process engineer, I want to select a global resolved model default, so that every new turn uses the model configuration I currently prefer.
3. As a process engineer, I want to change the global model default between turns, so that I can use different models for different reasoning tasks without creating a new chat.
4. As a process engineer, I want the selected model and provider route to be captured on each model invocation, so that I can understand what actually produced an outcome.
5. As a process engineer, I want a user message to become a durable turn task, so that work can resume after a process crash or application restart.
6. As a process engineer, I want PortLog invoked on demand for each turn, so that idle chats do not require long-lived harness processes.
7. As a process engineer, I want a turn to resume from persisted execution state, so that completed work is not repeated after a runtime is replaced.
8. As a process engineer, I want the harness to determine when a turn is complete, so that a model stopping its response does not falsely imply that the intended work is finished.
9. As a process engineer, I want deterministic validators, explicit terminal responses, policy limits, cancellation, and unrecoverable errors to contribute to turn completion state, so that completion and failure are observable and trustworthy.
10. As a process engineer, I want the model to choose tools semantically, so that PortLog can support process work without forcing every activity into a fixed operation-kind taxonomy.
11. As a process engineer, I want model inference, generic tool calls, and logic-program execution represented as distinct typed invocation targets, so that each can retain its own execution semantics while sharing lifecycle mechanics.
12. As a process engineer, I want logic-program results to be replayed when already completed, so that deterministic reasoning is not unnecessarily rerun during recovery.
13. As a process engineer, I want interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic invocations to follow target-specific retry rules, so that recovery is safe rather than blind replay.
14. As a process engineer, I want tool capabilities declared in a registry, so that PortLog can expose and govern available capabilities without inventing a complete process ontology first.
15. As a process engineer, I want each generic tool to declare capability scope and policy metadata, so that authorization and deterministic policy checks are enforced outside the model.
16. As a process engineer, I want PortLog to authorize and sequence agent-originated effects, so that the server cannot accidentally become a second agent runtime.
17. As a process engineer, I want server adapters to execute approved harness-directed capabilities, so that infrastructure remains reusable without owning agent decisions.
18. As a process engineer, I want no mandatory human approval gate for normal autonomous work, so that the harness can complete processes without waiting for manual confirmation.
19. As a process engineer, I want approval-free execution bounded by least-privilege identities and capability manifests, so that autonomy does not mean unrestricted access.
20. As a process engineer, I want deterministic policy gates evaluated before dispatch, so that prompts cannot override authorization or safety constraints.
21. As a process engineer, I want tool execution isolated by workspace, filesystem, process, network, and secret boundaries where applicable, so that model-produced actions cannot escape their intended environment.
22. As a process engineer, I want external side effects to use stable idempotency keys, so that retries do not duplicate irreversible work.
23. As a process engineer, I want unknown outcomes distinguished from failures, so that a lost connection after an external effect is reconciled before retrying.
24. As a process engineer, I want checkpoints at durable commit boundaries, so that recovery can resume from the last known safe point.
25. As a process engineer, I want bounded and classified retries with compensation where possible, so that failures do not create uncontrolled loops or inconsistent state.
26. As a process engineer, I want append-only audit evidence for autonomous execution, so that I can reconstruct identity, policy decisions, invocation attempts, effects, and recovery behavior.
27. As a process engineer, I want full raw model and tool payloads excluded by default, so that SQLite growth, sensitive-data retention, and provider coupling stay bounded.
28. As a process engineer, I want normalized semantic events and artifact references persisted, so that durable recovery and useful auditability do not require retaining every raw payload.
29. As a process engineer, I want transient model deltas streamed to the UI, so that responses feel live without storing every token durably.
30. As a process engineer, I want completed message boundaries, tool results, checkpoints, retries, failures, and completion transitions persisted, so that the UI and harness can recover meaningful state.
31. As a process engineer, I want SQLite and the durable event log to be authoritative, so that missed WebSocket messages cannot corrupt the chat state.
32. As a process engineer, I want the UI to rebuild durable state after reconnecting and then resume live delivery, so that an interrupted connection does not lose activity.
33. As a process engineer, I want conversation to remain the primary UI, so that execution details support the chat instead of replacing it with an operations dashboard.
34. As a process engineer, I want model, tool, and logic-program activity shown inline and expandable, so that I can inspect execution when useful without overwhelming the main conversation.
35. As a process engineer, I want unknown, retrying, failed, cancelled, and completed states visible in the activity view, so that the UI accurately communicates durable execution status.
36. As a process engineer, I want projects, chats, settings, persistence, and transport to remain available independently of a running harness, so that the application remains useful infrastructure rather than a collection of provider sessions.
37. As a process engineer, I want future governed domain actions introduced only when a concrete capability needs stronger semantics, so that PortLog can evolve its process ontology from real requirements instead of speculation.

## Implementation Decisions

- Replace provider-specific product identity with provider-neutral threads and durable turns.
- Treat each turn as a durable task whose execution is owned by one PortLog harness implementation and started on demand.
- Keep the harness runtime disposable. Recovery loads persisted turn state and the canonical event log rather than relying on a long-lived process.
- Make PortLog the sole complete agent-loop authority: context, model calls, tool selection, capability dispatch, logic programs, completion, checkpoints, cancellation, retries, and recovery.
- Keep the server as infrastructure: projects, threads, settings, credentials/configuration administration, SQLite mechanics, WebSocket transport, durable projections, and capability adapters.
- Store a global resolved model selection containing provider route, model ID, and relevant model settings. Resolve it at each turn and snapshot it into the model invocation.
- Do not retain a provider-owned thread/session model. Existing provider-specific development data is outside the target compatibility contract.
- Define one shared invocation lifecycle envelope with typed targets for `model`, `tool`, and `logic_program`. Do not add a universal `HarnessOperationKind`.
- Give invocations stable IDs and attempt numbers. Make event writes idempotent and append-only. Rebuild current-state projections from the event log.
- Persist semantic event boundaries, lifecycle state, checkpoints, normalized results, policy outcomes, usage/timing metadata, and artifact references. Stream token/delta detail transiently.
- Do not persist full raw model/tool payloads by default. Optional diagnostics/evaluation capture must be separately governed by retention and redaction controls.
- Replay completed deterministic logic-program invocations from their recorded result. Permit rerun only for interrupted or explicitly non-deterministic work under target-specific retry policy.
- Introduce a capability registry for generic tools. Each tool declares scope, policy metadata, input/output contract, execution adapter, idempotency behavior, and applicable isolation requirements.
- Enforce deterministic policy and authorization at the PortLog capability boundary, outside prompts. Use least-privilege capability manifests and scoped identities.
- Keep mandatory human approval disabled for normal autonomous execution. Preserve optional escalation, cancellation, intervention, and policy-based refusal as separate controls.
- Require reconciliation for unknown external outcomes before retry; use stable idempotency keys and durable commit markers for side effects.
- Use isolation, staging, dry-run, compensation, or reversal where the capability supports them; do not claim that every effect is reversible.
- Use SQLite/event log as the source of truth. WebSocket is a live delivery channel only; reconnect rebuilds durable state before continuing live updates.
- Project the UI in an OMP-style conversation-first view with inline expandable activity for model, tool, and logic-program invocations. Do not build a separate execution dashboard initially.
- Adapt existing provider runtime/orchestration consumers through compatibility projections during implementation only where needed to reach the new canonical harness contracts; the target model itself remains provider-neutral.
- Future first-class governed domain actions are deferred until a concrete process capability demonstrates the need for stronger authorization, validation, staging, or audit semantics.

## Testing Decisions

- Test the highest seam: submit a user turn through the PortLog turn boundary and observe durable SQLite state plus WebSocket-visible projections. Prefer end-to-end behavior over implementation-specific adapter tests.
- Verify that a turn resolves the global model selection per invocation and records an immutable execution snapshot without making the thread provider-owned.
- Verify restart/replacement recovery from persisted events and execution state, including no duplicate execution of completed invocations.
- Verify typed model/tool/logic-program invocation lifecycles, stable IDs, attempt numbers, idempotent event writes, deterministic replay, and target-specific retry behavior.
- Verify completion policy behavior for explicit completion, validator success/failure, waiting, cancellation, policy limits, unrecoverable errors, and unknown external outcomes.
- Verify capability registry scope and policy enforcement with allowed, denied, malformed, expired, and out-of-scope requests. Tests must prove prompts cannot bypass policy.
- Verify idempotency and reconciliation across timeout-after-effect, duplicate delivery, runtime crash, retry, and compensation scenarios.
- Verify audit output contains normalized attribution, policy inputs/outcomes, invocation attempts, side-effect references, and recovery transitions without requiring raw payload persistence.
- Verify transient streaming is not required for durable recovery, while semantic completion and tool-result boundaries are persisted.
- Verify WebSocket disconnect/reconnect rebuilds the conversation and expandable activity from SQLite/event projections, then resumes live delivery without duplication or loss.
- Verify the UI renders conversation-first output and expandable model/tool/logic-program activity, including retrying, unknown, failed, cancelled, and completed states.
- Reuse existing server integration-test patterns for WebSocket lifecycle, durable event repositories, orchestration projections, provider runtime ingress, and PortLog bridge smoke coverage. Add contract tests at the PortLog boundary rather than duplicating every provider adapter.
- Tests should assert externally observable state transitions, persisted records, emitted messages, and recovery behavior—not private functions, class structure, or the number of internal modules.

## Out of Scope

- Rebuilding the Paper chat design.
- Treating Claude, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, or any other runtime as the product identity of a thread.
- Maintaining a legacy provider-session compatibility layer for nonexistent users or old development data.
- A universal `HarnessOperationKind` taxonomy.
- A full Palantir-style process ontology or domain-action registry at initial launch.
- Mandatory human approval for every agent action.
- Persisting every model token or full raw model/tool payload by default.
- A separate execution dashboard before the conversation-first UI proves insufficient.
- Moving direct user-initiated infrastructure actions through PortLog when they are not agent-originated.
- Replacing projects, threads, SQLite, settings, or WebSocket infrastructure with a harness-owned product backend.

## Further Notes

The target is a clean-slate architecture for an early, not-yet-usable application; preserving old provider-specific development data is not a product requirement. The key design principle is “product on harness, harness on model”: PortLog owns the agent loop and durable execution authority, while the server provides durable application infrastructure and narrow capability adapters. The model supplies semantic reasoning and tool selection, including reasoning through logic programs; the harness supplies execution, policy, recovery, and evidence.

title: Establish the provider-neutral turn contract
description:
## Parent

pl-217.8 — Implement PortLog as the provider-neutral durable harness

## What to build

Create a durable turn for each user message. The turn must use the global model selection and expose its state through the server.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A user message creates one durable turn.
- [ ] The turn stores its lifecycle state.
- [ ] The turn uses the current global model selection.
- [ ] The turn has no provider identity.

## Blocked by

- None — can start immediately.

title: Persist and recover the invocation trace
description:
## Parent

pl-217.8 — Implement PortLog as the provider-neutral durable harness

## What to build

Save model, tool, and logic-program events for each turn. Resume interrupted work without repeating completed work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The system saves semantic events and checkpoints.
- [ ] Each invocation has a stable ID and attempt number.
- [ ] Recovery does not repeat a completed invocation.
- [ ] The system marks unknown outcomes separately from failures.

## Blocked by

- Establish the provider-neutral turn contract

title: Route turns through the PortLog harness
description:

pl-217.8 — Implement PortLog as the provider-neutral durable harness

## What to build

Make PortLog own the complete turn loop. PortLog must handle context, model calls, tool calls, logic programs, retries, cancellation, and completion checks.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each turn enters PortLog once.
- [ ] PortLog owns the turn state machine.
- [ ] PortLog resumes a turn after a runtime stops.
- [ ] The server does not run a second agent loop.

## Blocked by

- Persist and recover the invocation trace

title: Add the capability registry and tool dispatch
description:

Add a registry for generic tools. Each tool must declare its capability scope and policy data. PortLog must check this data before dispatch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The registry lists available tools.
- [ ] Each tool declares its capability scope.
- [ ] PortLog checks policy before tool dispatch.
- [ ] The server runs tools only through PortLog requests.

## Blocked by

- Route turns through the PortLog harness

title: Add autonomous execution controls

- [ ] Tools use scoped identities and capability limits.
- [ ] External effects use idempotency keys.
- [ ] Unknown outcomes trigger reconciliation before retry.
